To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the initial decline in the hemoglobin level during neoadjuviant hormonal therapy was a predictor of PSA failure following radiation therapy and androgen suppression therapy.

1) the initial decline in Hgb during neoadjuvanthormonal therapy predicts for early PSA failure following radiation and AST for patients with intermediate- and high-risk prostate cancer and 2) a Hgb nadir level of <11 g/dl during AST was also predictive for PSA failure.

the rate of decline of Hgb levels during neoadjuviant hormonal therapy predicts for PSA failure following radiation therapy and hormonal therapy in patients with intermediate and/or high-risk prostate cancer.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of the relationship between the rate of decline of hemoglobin (Hb) levels during neoadjuvanthormonal therapy (NHT) and the subsequent PSA failure following external beam radiotherapy (EBRT).

the study of the effects of the administration of androgen suppression on the rate of decline of hemoglobin and the relationship of this decline to early prostate specific antigen (P.S.A.) failure in men receiving external radiation and hormone treatment.
the use of the serum Hgb level as a marker of the response of prostate cancer to treatment with AST.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a significant decline in Hgb levels during neoadjuvast treatment predicts for early PSA failure following RT.
the Hgb level is not a useful prognostic factor in prostate cancer patients treated with RT and AST.
the use of neoadjuvanat AST in prostate cancer is associated with a significant decline in the serum Hgb level.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Hgb level is not a useful predictor for early PSA failure following radiation and AST for intermediate and high-risk prostate cancer.
Hgb decline during AST was predictive of time to PSA failure following RT and AST, but that the Hgb level alone was not predictive.
the initial rate of decline in Hgb level following neoadjuvant therapy predicts for early PSA failure.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the decline in the HGB level is a predictor of early PSA failure following the use of RT and AST for patients with intermediate‐ and high‐risk disease.

the rate of hemoglobin decline in the setting of neoadjuviant hormonal therapy is a useful predictor of PSA failure in men with intermediate or high risk prostate cancer who are treated with external beam radiation therapy and hormonal therapy.
the rate of change of the Hgb level is a useful prognostic indicator of time to PSA failure.
